reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
clinicalPearls: The core deformity is lateral (valgus) deviation of the great toe at the first metatarsophalangeal joint combined with medial deviation of the first metatarsal (metatarsus primus varus)
The prominent medial eminence forms the visible bunion and often develops an inflamed adventitial bursa that causes pain against footwear
Deformity is commoner in women and is associated with constricting or high-heeled shoes, a positive family history, ligamentous laxity, and pes planus
Progression involves attenuation of the medial capsule, lateral displacement of the sesamoids, and a bowstringing pull of the extrinsic tendons that perpetuates the drift
Assess the whole first ray for mobility and for a second-toe crossover or transfer metatarsalgia, and always examine standing
Weight-bearing radiographs allow measurement of the hallux valgus and intermetatarsal angles and grading of first metatarsophalangeal joint congruence and arthritis
Initial management is conservative with wide, soft, low-heeled footwear, toe spacers, bunion pads, and orthoses; surgery is reserved for persistent pain not for cosmesis
Surgical options are tailored to deformity severity and joint condition and include distal or proximal metatarsal osteotomy, soft-tissue realignment, and first metatarsophalangeal arthrodesis
reference.pathophysiology: Hallux valgus is a progressive deformity in which the great toe deviates laterally at the first metatarsophalangeal joint while the first metatarsal drifts medially into varus. As the proximal phalanx pulls into valgus, the medial capsule and collateral ligament stretch and the lateral structures contract, and the sesamoid complex is left behind laterally relative to the metatarsal head. The long flexor and extensor tendons then act eccentric to the joint axis and bowstring across it, generating a deforming force that drives further progression. Intrinsic predispositions such as a mobile or hypermobile first ray, a flat foot, generalised ligamentous laxity, and inherited foot shape combine with extrinsic pressure from narrow, elevated-heel footwear. The exposed medial eminence rubs against the shoe, producing a painful inflamed bursa, while altered load transfer can overload the lesser rays and produce transfer metatarsalgia.
additionalDifferentials: Hallux rigidus with first metatarsophalangeal osteoarthritis
Gout or other crystal arthropathy of the first metatarsophalangeal joint
Inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid or psoriatic disease affecting the forefoot
First metatarsophalangeal joint sesamoiditis or sesamoid disorders
Ganglion or soft-tissue swelling over the medial eminence
Septic arthritis or infected bursa of the first metatarsophalangeal joint
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing dorsoplantar and lateral foot radiographs to measure the hallux valgus and intermetatarsal angles
Assessment of first metatarsophalangeal joint congruence, sesamoid position, and degenerative change on radiographs
Standing clinical examination for first-ray mobility, associated lesser-toe deformity, and transfer metatarsalgia
Pedobarography or plantar pressure mapping where forefoot overload is suspected
Serum urate and inflammatory markers if crystal or inflammatory arthropathy is considered
Vascular and neurological assessment before any planned surgical correction
Cross-sectional imaging only in atypical cases to characterise soft-tissue masses or occult pathology
redFlags: Hot, swollen, exquisitely tender joint suggesting septic arthritis, an infected bursa, or acute gout rather than uncomplicated deformity
Rapidly progressive or symmetrical forefoot deformity indicating underlying inflammatory arthritis
Ulceration, skin breakdown, or signs of ischaemia over the medial eminence, particularly in diabetes or peripheral vascular disease
Neurological symptoms or a cavus foot pointing to an underlying neuromuscular disorder
Sudden severe pain with an inability to bear weight suggesting fracture or acute joint pathology
reference.prognosis: Hallux valgus tends to progress slowly over years, and conservative measures relieve symptoms but do not reverse the bony deformity. Appropriately selected surgery corrects alignment and relieves pain in the majority, though recurrence, stiffness, transfer metatarsalgia, or under- or over-correction can occur, and outcomes are poorer when surgery is performed for appearance alone or in the presence of untreated hypermobility or inflammatory disease.
pitfalls: Operating for cosmetic reasons rather than pain, which risks a dissatisfied patient with a stiff or recurrent deformity
Failing to measure the intermetatarsal angle so that an osteotomy inadequate for the deformity is chosen and recurrence follows
Overlooking first-ray hypermobility or an underlying flat foot that predisposes to failure of correction
Missing associated lesser-toe deformity or transfer metatarsalgia that will continue to cause pain after bunion surgery
Attributing a hot painful joint to the bunion and missing gout, infection, or inflammatory arthritis
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
